match.reason: None of the bank points teaches how a text's characters, relationships, settings, plot twists and point of view work together; the closest, writing about experience and the text, covers paragraph structure and linking a technique to its effect, not this interplay of elements.

draft.title: The dynamics of a text
card: The dynamics of a text are the parts that move the story and shape its meaning. They include motives, relationships, setting, plot and point of view.
Motive
the reason a character acts. Tension in a relationship, such as a clash of wants between two people, often grows from different motives.
Setting and plot
setting is the time and place, and it can press on characters or reveal their values. A twist is a sudden turn in the plot that changes what the reader expects.
Point of view
the view from which events are told. A narrator who sees only one character's thoughts can make the reader trust or doubt that character. These parts work together, so a good essay links them.
draft.remember: Motives, relationships, setting, plot and point of view act together to build meaning.

a.q: Which of these best describes a character's motive?
opts: The reason the character chooses to act
The place where the character lives
The person who tells the story
A sudden turn that surprises the reader
a.why: A motive is the reason behind a character's actions. The place is the setting, the teller is the point of view, and a sudden turn is a twist in the plot.
a.clue: Think about why a character does something.

b.q: In a story set in a drought-hit town, a farmer, Ana, wants to sell up while her brother wants to stay. Their quarrel grows as the dry weather worsens. Which pair of dynamics is being used?
opts: Tension in a relationship and the pressure of setting
A plot twist and a change in point of view
A narrator's bias and a character's costume
The text's form and the writer's historical context
b.why: The quarrel between Ana and her brother is tension in a relationship, and the drought is a setting that presses on them. Nothing in the scenario is a twist or a shift in who tells the story, so the other pairs do not fit.
b.clue: Look for the quarrel and the place it happens in.

a.best: The reason the character chooses to act

b.best: Tension in a relationship and the pressure of setting

problems.detail: The clue 'Look for the quarrel and the place it happens in' points straight at the two halves of the right option (quarrel = relationship tension, place = setting), so a student can match it without understanding the dynamics.

The why says 'the teller is the point of view', but the card defines point of view as 'the view from which events are told'. The person who tells the story is the narrator, so this blurs narrator and point of view.

check.summary: Both questions are correct and keyed well. The clue for (b) nearly gives the answer away, and the why for (a) loosely equates the narrator with point of view.
